ἐκπέμψαι καὶ ἰδεῖν, εἰ καὶ ἀληθῆ τὰ λεγόμενα. Ἐν τούτοις οὖν ὁ χρόνος ἐτρίβετο.
Πρὸς δὴ τούτοις, ὅτε τὸ ἀληθὲς ἔγνωσαν, βασιλεῖς ὄντες καὶ ἐκδημεῖν μέλλοντες,
ἀνάγκην εἶχον πρότερον εὖ διαθεῖναι τὰ κατὰ τὸν οἶκον, καὶ ἐπιστῆσαι τοῖς
ἀρχομένοις τοὺς ἀνθ' ἑαυτῶν. Ταῦτα πάντα αὐτοὺς ἀπησχόλει, καὶ ἐνε βράδυνον.
Καὶ εἰ μὴ σφόδρα γε ἀγαπητοί τινες ἦσαν καὶ δίκαιοι, οὐκ ἂν, τὰς οἰκείας
καταλιπόντες χώρας καὶ βασιλείας, ἀφικνοῦντο πρὸς τὴν ἐπίσκεψιν, ἀλλὰ δι'
ἑτέρων τὴν χρείαν ἐπλήρουν. Ἔστι δὲ ἐννοεῖν, ὡς καὶ οἰκονομία τις ἦν θεία τῆς
ἀφίξεως ἡ ἀναβολή. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ὁμοῦ τῇ τῶν φίλων διαλέξει καὶ τὸ πᾶν τοῦ ἀγῶνος
ἐλύθη, τοῦ Θεοῦ χρηματίσαντος, καὶ τὸν δίκαιον ἀνακτησαμένου καὶ
στεφανώσαντος, οἰκονο μία τις γέγονε θεία, ἐμβραδῦναι τοὺς φίλους, ἵνα παραταθῇ
τὰ τοῦ νοσήματος, καὶ μειζόνως ἀθλή σας ὁ δίκαιος, δικαιότερον ἀναῤῥηθῇ παρὰ τοῦ
Θεοῦ. Στίχ. ιαʹ. Καὶ παρεγένοντο πρὸς αὐτὸν ὁμοθυ μαδὸν, τοῦ παρακαλέσαι καὶ
ἐπισκέψασθαι αὐτόν. Ὁ Σύμμαχος οὕτως ἐξέδωκε· Συνετάξαντο γὰρ ὁμοῦ ἐλθόντες
συμπαθῆσαι αὐτῷ, καὶ παραμυ θήσασθαι αὐτόν. Ὅρα καὶ ἐντεῦθεν, ὡς καὶ ἕτερος
παρῆλθε χρόνος, ἕως ὅτε, πρὸς ἀλλήλους διαπεμψά μενοι, τὴν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ σύνοδόν
τε καὶ ἄφιξιν ἐποιή σαντο. Στίχ. ιβʹ. Καὶ καταπασάμενοι γῆν ἐπὶ τὰς κεφαλὰς αὐτῶν.
Στίχ. ιγʹ. Παρεκάθισαν αὐτῷ ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας, καὶ ἑπτὰ νύκτας. Οὐκ εἶπε δὲ ἡ Γραφὴ, ὅτι
παρεκάθηντο ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας πρωΐθεν ἕως ἑσπέρας, οὐδὲ ἑπτὰ νύκτας ἀφ' ἑσπέρας
μέχρι πρωΐ. ∆ῆλον οὖν, ὅτι, τὸ πλεῖον τῆς ἡμέρας παρακαθεζόμενοι, ὑπεχώρουν τὰς
ἀναγκαίας ἐκπληρώσοντες χρείας· καὶ πάλιν ἐπανήκοντες, μέ χρι πολλοῦ τῆς νυκτὸς
παρεκαθέζοντο, καὶ αὖθις ἀπιόντες, πάλιν ὤρθριζον πρὸς αὐτόν. Ὃ δὴ τῶν
γνησιωτάτων καὶ συμπαθεστάτων φίλων ἴδιον. Τῇ δὲ κοινῇ συνηθείᾳ χρωμένη ἡ
Γραφὴ, οὕτως ἀπολύτως εἶπε· Παρεκάθισαν αὐτῷ ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας καὶ ἑπτὰ νύκτας. Ἐπεὶ
καὶ ὅτε λέγει τὸν Ἰακὼβ δεκατέσσαρα ἔτη δουλεῦσαι, καὶ συγκαίεσθαι τῷ καύσονι
τῆς ἡμέρας καὶ τῷ παγετῷ τῆς νυκτὸς, ἆρα ὑπὸ στέ γην οὐκ εἰσῄει ποτέ; ἆρα
οὐδεμιᾶς ἀναπαύσεως ἔτυχεν ὅλῳ τῷ χρόνῳ; Ταῦτα μὲν οὖν καὶ λεπτολο γεῖν
φλύαρον. Ὡς γὰρ ἔφην, ἡ Γραφὴ κοινῇ συνη θείᾳ χρῆται. Ἐπειδὴ δέ τινες,
κωμῳδοῦντες τὴν Γραφὴν, καὶ ἐντεῦθεν αὐτὴν ὡς ψευδῆ διασύρουσιν· Ὡς γὰρ ἂν,
φασὶν, ἄσιτοι διετέλουν καὶ ἄϋπνοι ἐπὶ τοσαύταις ἡμέραις; ἠναγκάσθημεν αὐτῶν
συνα παχθῆναι τῇ ἀκαίρῳ στενοχωρίᾳ. ΚΕΦ. Γʹ. Ἀλλ' ἐν τούτοις μὲν τὸ δεύτερον
ἤνυσται κεφά λαιον· τοῦ τρίτου δὲ προθεωρίαν ποιούμενοι, φαμὲν, 17.68 ὡς ἀλγεῖ
μὲν ὁ δίκαιος, καὶ οὐκ ἄν τις ἀρνήσαιτο οὐ γὰρ τῶν ἀναισθήτων ἡ ἀρετὴ, ἀλλὰ τῶν
ἐν τοῖς πάθεσι φιλοσοφούντων. Οὐ δύναται δὲ, κατὰ μὲν τὸ φαινόμενον, ὑπὸ τῆς ἐν
σαρκὶ πληγῆς δριμυ τάτως κεντούμενος· κατὰ δὲ τὸ νοούμενον, οἷα δί καιος καὶ
φιλόθεος ἀνὴρ ὁρῶν τινας σκανδαλιζομέ νους ἐπὶ τοῖς αὐτῶν παθήμασιν, ὡς τῆς τοῦ
Θεοῦ δόξης ἐπ' αὐτῷ διασυρομένης, εἰ ὁ δίκαιος ταῦτα ὑπομένει. Καὶ γὰρ ὅτε λέγει·
Ἵνα τί ἔθου με κατ' ἐντευκτήν σου; οὐκ αὐτὸς κατὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐτύγχανε, μὴ γένοιτο!
τίνι γὰρ εἶχεν ἐντυγχάνειν; Ἀλλὰ τοῦτό ἐστιν ὅ φησιν· Ἵνα τί δι' ἐμὲ, ∆έσποτα, τὸ
ὄνομά σου βλασφημεῖται; Θορυβεῖται δὲ οὐδὲν ἧττον καὶ ἰλιγγιᾷ, μήπως πλείως
ἐγκατάλειψιν ὑπέστη παρὰ Θεοῦ. Οὐδὲ γὰρ οὕτω τιμωρεῖται ψυχὴ φιλόθεος, ὡς τὸ
ὑποπτεύειν καταλελεῖφθαι παρὰ Θεοῦ· καὶ μυριάκις αἱρεῖται τὸν θάνατον, ἢ μετὰ
ἀλγηδόνων καὶ τοιαύτης ὑποψίας τοῖς ζῶσιν ἐγκατα λέγεσθαι. Ἐπὶ μὲν οὖν τῇ τῶν
κτημάτων ἀπωλείᾳ καὶ τῇ τῶν παίδων ἀθρόᾳ τελευτῇ οἵας ἀφῆκε χα ριστηρίους
φωνὰς ἠκούσαμεν, καὶ ὅπως τὴν γυναῖκα ἐξεπαίδευσεν ἀπρεπές τι περὶ τοῦ
∆εσπότου λογισα μένην, καὶ ποῖα μετὰ πεῖραν καὶ ἐξουδένωσιν καὶ τὸ δριμὺ πάθος
ἐφθέγξατο, καὶ ὡς οὐδὲν αὐτὸν τῶν ἀν θρωπίνων συμπτωμάτων διεθορύβησεν· ὡς
δὲ οἱ φί λοι παρεγένοντο ἄνδρες δίκαιοι καὶ συμπαθεῖς, εὔ καιρον ᾠήθη, θεωρῶν
αὐτῶν τὴν ὑπομονὴν καὶ τὴν ἀγάπην ἐπ' αὐτῶν, εἰπεῖν καὶ δημοσιεῦσαι τὰς κατὰ
ψυχὴν ἀλγηδόνας, καὶ φθέγγεται μὲν καθ' ἱστο ρίαν ἀκίνδυνον. Ἓν γὰρ ἦν τοῦ

And they waited to confirm the report through more people, or also to send out and see whether the things said were also true. In these things, then, time was spent. In addition to these, when they knew the truth, being kings and about to go abroad, they had necessity first to set the things of the house well in order, and to appoint over the ruled those in their place. All these things occupied them, and they delayed. And if they had not been exceedingly beloved and righteous, they would not, leaving their own countries and kingdoms, have arrived for the visit, but would have filled the need through others. And one may think that there was also some divine arrangement of the delay of the arrival. For since together with the friends’ dialogue the whole contest was also dissolved, God having spoken oracle and having recovered and crowned the righteous one, some divine arrangement happened, for the friends to delay, so that the things of the illness might be prolonged, and the righteous one, having contended more greatly, might be proclaimed more justly by God. Verse 11: And they came to him with one mind, to comfort and visit him. Symmachus rendered thus: For they arranged together, having come, to sympathize with him and comfort him. See also from here that another time also passed, until, having sent messages to one another, they made the gathering to the same place and the arrival. Verse 12: And having sprinkled earth upon their heads. Verse 13: They sat beside him seven days and seven nights. But Scripture did not say that they sat beside seven days from morning until evening, nor seven nights from evening until morning. Clear, then, that sitting beside for the greater part of the day, they withdrew to fulfill necessary needs; and coming back again, they sat beside until late in the night, and going away again, they rose early again toward him. Which is proper to the most genuine and most sympathetic friends. And Scripture, using common custom, said thus absolutely: They sat beside him seven days and seven nights. Since also when it says Jacob served fourteen years, and was burned with the heat of day and the frost of night, did he never go under a roof? Did he meet no rest in the whole time? These things, then, even to quibble about is nonsense. For as I said, Scripture uses common custom. But since some, mocking Scripture, from here also tear it as false — For how, they say, would they continue without food and without sleep for so many days? — we were forced to be led along with their untimely distress. Chapter 3: But in these things the second chapter has been completed; and making a preliminary view of the third, we say, 17.68 that the righteous one feels pain, and no one would deny it — for virtue is not of the unfeeling, but of those who philosophize in the passions. And he cannot, according to what appears, being stung most sharply by the blow in the flesh; and according to what is thought, as a righteous and God-loving man seeing some scandalized at their sufferings, as the glory of God being torn against him if the righteous one endures these things. For when he says: Why have you set me as your opponent in prayer? he himself was not hitting against God — far be it! For to whom would he have to make petition? But this is what he says: Why, through me, Master, is your name blasphemed? And he is disturbed no less and grows dizzy, lest he have undergone a greater abandonment from God. For a God-loving soul is not punished so much as by suspecting it has been left by God; and ten thousand times it chooses death rather than to be enrolled among the living with pains and such a suspicion. So at the loss of possessions and the sudden death of the children we heard what thanksgiving voices he sent up, and how he educated the wife who had thought something unseemly about the Master, and what things he spoke after trial and contempt and the sharp passion, and that none of human accidents disturbed him; but when the friends arrived, righteous and sympathetic men, he thought it timely, seeing their endurance and love toward him, to speak and publish the pains according to the soul, and he speaks according to a history without danger. pass_b_english: paradox of the calamity also seemed unbelievable — Job on a dunghill and uncared for. They waited to confirm the report through more witnesses, or to send and see if it was true; time was spent that way. Once they knew the truth, as kings about to travel they first had to set their houses in order and appoint deputies. That occupied them and delayed them. Had they not been deeply beloved and righteous, they would not have left countries and kingdoms to visit, but would have sent others. One may also see a divine arrangement in the delay: since the friends’ dialogue ends the whole contest when God speaks, recovers, and crowns the righteous man, the friends’ lateness stretches the illness so that, contending more, he may be declared more justly by God.

"[[They came to him with one mind to comfort and visit him >> Bible:Job 2:11]]." Symmachus: they arranged together to sympathize and comfort. Another stretch of time passed while they messaged one another and set a common arrival. "[[They sprinkled earth on their heads >> Bible:Job 2:12]]." "[[They sat beside him seven days and seven nights >> Bible:Job 2:13]]." Scripture does not mean continuous day-from-dawn and night-from-dusk without break. They sat the greater part of the day, withdrew for necessary needs, returned late into the night, left again, and rose early to him — the mark of genuine friends. Scripture speaks by common custom, as when Jacob served fourteen years burned by day heat and night frost without meaning he never entered a roof. Quibbling further is nonsense. Some mock Scripture as false — "How without food and sleep for so many days?" — and we are forced to answer their untimely distress.

Chapter 3 begins: the righteous man feels pain — no one denies it. Virtue is not numbness, but philosophy inside the passions. In appearance he is stung sharply in the flesh; in thought, as a God-loving man, he sees others scandalized at such sufferings, as if God’s glory were torn if the righteous endure this. When he says, "[[Why have you set me as your opponent in prayer? >> Bible:Job 7:20]]," he is not striking at God — far from it. To whom else would he petition? He means: Why, through me, Master, is your name blasphemed? He also grows dizzy lest abandonment from God be greater still. A God-loving soul suffers nothing like the suspicion of being left by God, and chooses death ten thousand times over life under that suspicion.
